source.title: What do VLM-Based Vision-Language Navigation Models Rely on: Interpreting and Steering Policy Behavior
source.authors: Débora Oliveira Makowski; Samiran Gode; Abhijeet Nayak; Marco Hutter; Cordelia Schmid; Lukas Schmid; Wolfram Burgard

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study uses feed-forward neurons and their value vectors as units for semantic analysis and behavioral steering, but it does not test whether neuron poles generally have one main job or whether explanations predict activation on held-out inputs.
record.gate_note: The paper measures token-associated value vectors and reports neuron-clamping effects on navigation motion, included below as related results that fit no claim version. Its other input-sensitivity, activation-vector reasoning-steering, and navigation-success results do not test the listed neuron-explanation claims.
record.test_reason: The paper uses FFN value vectors, labelled by their top-20 vocabulary tokens following Geva et al., as steering handles in VLN models. It never estimates how many neurons have one or more jobs. It does not score neuron explanations against held-out activations, build neuron attribution graphs, or compare interpretable-neuron shares across architectures or tools. Its other results (input-attribution precision, memory sensitivity, reasoning steering) concern policy inputs and behaviour, not neuron explanation.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate but incomplete. The authors also conclude that VLN policies are sensitive to all input modalities, with ~40–60% attribution precision on human-annotated cues. They find no apparent link between sensitivity and success rate. Steering raised AwareVLN's real-world success from 37.2% to 74.4%.
record.recipe_differences: Uses value-vector token associations and activation clamping/steering to influence VLN behavior; it does not generate and test neuron explanations or audit pole-level job counts.
record.method_sensitivity: not stated for the listed neuron-explanation claims.

fits_no_version.finding: Value vectors whose top-20 vocabulary tokens include navigation words persist after VLN fine-tuning of Qwen2.5-VL. Clamping those neurons shifts DualVLN's motion-token frequencies toward the clamped concept (5 episodes).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In VLM-based VLN policies, FFN neurons labelled by vocabulary projection of their value vectors retain pretrained navigation concepts after fine-tuning, and clamping them causally biases motion behaviour.

record.problems: The paper does not test the listed neuron-explanation claims. The neuron-clamping experiment covers 5 episodes, and the supplied flattened Table IV text makes the alignment of its values to steering conditions unclear.
record.rows_left_out: No additional results bearing on the claim's neuron-explanation subject were left out.

untested.parts: No audit of neuron-pole job shares in Qwen3-32B or any model.
No cross-model or cross-scale shares of interpretable neurons; only DualVLN vs Qwen2.5-VL token-associated value-vector counts.
No vision-model polysemantic neurons, pose, or recursive generalization.
No estimate of interpretable-neuron share as a function of architecture, regularization or tools.
No attribution graphs built from neurons; no replacement-model comparison.
Neuron labels come from top-k vocabulary projections; there is no test of whether they predict where neurons fire.
No simulation-based scoring of neuron explanations.

record.verdict_notes: This is a robotics interpretability paper. Neuron-level content is limited to Geva-style value-vector token labels used as steering handles. Nothing bears on the share or quality of neuron explanations. The record's 'uncertainty_reported: y' applies only to Table V reasoning frequency; Table IV clamping has no uncertainty.

versions.untested_parts: Does not estimate the shares of poles with one job, two related jobs, or not-yet-understood jobs.
Does not compare pole-level job shares across model families or scales up to trillions of parameters.
Does not study InceptionV1 cat-and-car neurons, pose, or recursive generalization.
Does not estimate interpretable-neuron shares across architectures, regularization choices, or tools.
Does not build attribution graphs or test whether neuron-based graphs explain behavior without a replacement model.
Does not test explanations against activation locations on examples not used to write them.
Does not score neuron explanations by simulating activations on new text.

rows.subject: DualVLN
rows.operation_detail: Clamp selected FFN neuron input activations to prescribed values for positive and negative motion concepts.

conditions.value: forward versus turn; right versus left

rows.measure: Change in motion tokens under neuron clamping
rows.value: Table IV values, as flattened in the text: Forward +3.2%, +0.8%; Right −0.8%, −3.0%; Left −19.3%, +7.8%. The text extraction does not clearly preserve the column-to-condition alignment.
rows.note: The authors state that clamping biases navigation toward the corresponding semantic behaviors. The table layout in the supplied text does not unambiguously assign each number to a steering condition.
rows.check: Bears on no version: a clamping effect on motion tokens, not a neuron-job share or an explanation-prediction test. A plausible reading of the flattened Table IV puts one steering condition per row. Under forward-vs-turn, Forward is +3.2%, Right −0.8% and Left −19.3%. Under left+/right−, Forward is +0.8%, Right −3.0% and Left +7.8%. This reading is an inference, not stated alignment. The baseline is the unclamped policy, with no variance reported; n=5 episodes.

rows.subject: DualVLN
rows.operation_detail: Count per layer the value vectors whose top-20 vocabulary tokens correspond to selected textual or symbolic navigation tokens; compare with the original Qwen2.5-VL.

conditions.value: forward, left, right, stop, and arrow symbols

rows.measure: Percentage/count of value vectors associated with navigation tokens per layer
rows.value: figure only; the text states that the concepts are retained after fine-tuning, that symbolic-token activation is smaller for DualVLN only in the 5th layer, and that last-layer activation is increased for the verbal stop output.
rows.note: This measures token-associated value vectors, not the fraction of neuron poles with one or more jobs.
rows.check: Bears on no version. It counts value vectors whose top-20 output tokens include navigation tokens; it is not a share of neurons with one main job. The values are figure-only, so state relative to the claim cannot be read.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
